newsitem.title: JAPAN: Most Japanese unfamiliar with new voting system.
newsitem.headline: Most Japanese unfamiliar with new voting system.

text.p: A majority of Japanese are not familiar with the new electoral system to be introduced in the October 20 general elections, according to a media poll published on Saturday.

The poll by the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper of 3,000 eligible voters, conducted late last month, said 61 percent responded they were not familiar with the new electoral system, which combines single-seat constituencies with regional proportional representation.

The poll showed 72 percent of women were not familiar with the new system, which replaced the decades-old multi-member constituencies returning between three and five members to the Lower House of parliament.
The Yomiuri poll also said more than 70 percent of voters in their 20s did not know of the new electoral system, where voters would receive two ballots -- one for a candidate and one for a party.

The new chamber, the decisive of the two houses in Japan's parliament, will have 500 members, 300 elected in single-seat constituencies by candidate and 200 through proportional representation by party in 11 regional blocs.
The combined system has become complicated because a candidate can list himself in both domains -- the constituency and the proportional representation.
For example, a candidate who lost in a constituency can still be elected if the candidate's name is high on the party's submitted list of regional proportional representation.
The existing system was blamed as a root cause of expensive election campaigning which bred funding scandals.

Asked which party they would vote for in the constituencies, 32.7 percent of respondents said they would cast ballots for candidates in Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).

This was followed by 8.1 for the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), 5.2 for the new Democratic Party, and 4.9 for the Social Democrats led by outgoing Lower House speaker Takako Doi. A weighty 38.1 percent said they were undecided.

In the proportional representation blocs, 33.2 percent said they would vote LDP, followed by 8.0 for Shinshinto, 7.5 for the Democrats, 5.6 for the Socialists and 4.9 for the Japan Communist Party. Here again, 38.7 percent of the respondents were undecided.
Only 45 percent of respondents said they would vote for the same party in both ballots.
Asked who they would like to see as the new prime minister after elections, incumbent Hashimoto led by receiving 29.1 percent support.

This was followed by 13.7 for Naoto Kan, the outgoing health minister who spearheaded probes into a widespread AIDS scandal and star of the new Democratic Party, and 11.3 percent for Takako Doi, the fiery Socialist leader.
